name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
title: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
answer: Drafting proposals from past work is the practice of reusing and adapting earlier grant applications, progress reports, papers, and related documents to build a new funding request. It covers the narrative, aims, methods, preliminary data, budgets, timelines, biosketches, and compliance sections that funders require. The source material can include the researcher's own publications, prior submissions, reviewer comments, and institutional records. On this site, that past work can include the 135 research papers in the library, which provide reusable descriptions of methods, results, and gaps.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work is the practice of reusing and adapting earlier grant applications, progress reports, papers, and related documents to build a new funding request. It covers the narrative, aims, methods, preliminary data, budgets, timelines, biosketches, and compliance sections that funders require. The source material can include the researcher's own publications, prior submissions, reviewer comments, and institutional records. On this site, that past work can include the 135 research papers in the library, which provide reusable descriptions of methods, results, and gaps.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on document repositories, version control, reference managers, and the funder's own submission portal. It also depends on templates, checklists, and grant management systems that track deadlines, award numbers, and reporting requirements. Retrieval tools index past proposals and papers so that sections can be found and compared. Collaborative word processors and citation managers keep co-authors aligned on a single source of truth.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with gathering past proposals, papers, and reviews, then mapping their sections to the new call's requirements. Writers extract reusable text, update aims and methods, refresh preliminary data, and adjust the budget and timeline. They compare the new draft against the funder's rubric and use internal review to catch gaps. The site's 11795 extracted claims can be searched to locate prior results and gaps that support the new narrative. Generative assistants may summarize or suggest text, but a human checks every claim against the original source.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on provenance, attribution, and the funder's rules about resubmission and overlapping proposals. Practitioners track which text came from which source, check copyright and licensing for third-party material, and keep reviewer comments confidential. Risks include self-plagiarism, stale preliminary data, inaccurate claims, and undisclosed use of generative tools. Institutions and funders often require disclosure of AI assistance and may audit submissions for originality. Provenance records, version histories, and clear citations help show that reused material is legitimate and traceable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more structured reuse, with funders moving to machine-readable requirements and automated compliance checks. Retrieval systems will likely connect past proposals, publications, and institutional repositories through persistent identifiers. AI assistants may draft sections from past work, but human review and provenance tracking will remain central. Expect tighter scrutiny of originality, disclosure of AI use, and clearer rules on what can be recycled across submissions.
